property_summary: For any deployed C instance, owner() always returns the address stored in the first immutable argument slot (offset 0x0); the mutant returns the address from offset 0x14 instead, causing owner() to sometimes differ.

For any calldata bytes packed as the clone's immutable args, the reference contract's owner() equals the address encoded at offset 0x0 of the immutable args; the mutant instead reads offset 0x14 and thus for some immutable arg contents the returned owner differs.

For any calldata used as immutable args when cloning C, owner() always returns the address encoded at offset 0x0 of the immutable args; the mutant returns the address from offset 0x14 instead, so for some immutable-args bytes the returned owner differs.

For any deployed C clone initialized with immutable args bytes, the reference's owner() always returns the address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x00 (the first encoded address); the mutant reads from offset 0x14 and thus for some immutable-args bytes the returned owner() differs.

For any immutable-args byte array used when creating a clone of C, owner() must return the address encoded at offset 0x00 of those immutable args; the mutant instead reads offset 0x14 and thus for some immutable-args bytes owner() returns a different address.

For every deployment of the correct contract C, owner() returns the immutable address encoded at construction (i.e. a nonzero address when that immutable arg is nonzero); the mutant returns address(0) regardless, so there exist inputs where owner() != address(0) and thus differs.

For every deployed reference C, owner() returns the immutable owner address encoded at deployment (thus can be nonzero for many fuzzed addresses); the mutant always returns address(0), so there exist fuzzed owner addresses where owner() != address(0) and the mutant breaks the rule.

For any non-zero address A passed as the encoded immutable owner when deploying C, calling owner() on the deployed contract returns that same non-zero address (i.e. owner() != address(0)); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this rule for those inputs.

For any deployed C whose embedded immutable owner arg equals the factory-provided cooler owner address, calling owner() on that deployed instance returns the same nonzero address; the mutant that returns address(0) breaks this by making owner() = address(0) for some (nonzero) embedded owner inputs.

For any deployed C instance, calling owner() never returns the zero address iff the immutable owner argument used at deployment is non-zero; the reference preserves a non-zero owner when constructed with a non-zero address, whereas the mutant always returns address(0) and thus violates this for some fuzzed non-zero owner input.

For any deployed C, owner() always returns the immutable address encoded at the first immutable arg (the original owner address); the mutant returns the collateral address instead, so there exist inputs where owner() != collateral(), which breaks the rule.

For every deployed C, owner() must equal the first immutable arg embedded in the clone (the original owner address); the mutant instead returns address(collateral()), so there exist inputs where owner() != collateral(), causing the property to fail.

For any deployed C, owner() must equal the first immutable argument embedded in the clone (the owner immutable); the mutant makes owner() return address(collateral()) instead, so there exist inputs where owner() != collateral(), violating this rule.

For any deployed C clone, owner() must always equal the first immutable argument embedded in the contract (the owner address); the mutant returns address(collateral()) instead, so for some immutable args (owner != collateral) the mutant will return a different address and violate the property.

For any deployed C instance, owner() always equals collateral() only when the owner immutable was initialized to the collateral address; the reference never enforces owner()==address(collateral()), but the mutant makes owner() return address(collateral()), so there exist fuzzed immutable args (owner != collateral) for which the mutant's owner() differs — property: owner() == address(collateral()) holds if and only if the embedded owner immutable equals the embedded collateral immutable; the reference preserves the owner immutable so for arbitrary fuzzed owner and collateral inputs owner() == address(collateral()) is not guaranteed, but we instead assert the complementary universal rule that owner() != address(collateral()) for at least one admissible input is not acceptable — to make a universal property that the reference satisfies for all inputs and mutant breaks for some, we require that reading owner() does NOT equal address(collateral()) whenever the two immutable args differ; the reference returns the first immutable (owner arg) so when the two immutables differ owner() != address(collateral()) holds for all inputs where the two immutables differ, whereas the mutant returns address(collateral()) and thus will make owner()==address(collateral()) when immutables differ, violating the rule.

For any deployed C, collateral() returns the immutable argument stored at offset 0x14 inside the clone's immutable args; the mutant returns the value at 0x10, so for some immutable args layouts the returned address will differ causing collateral() to return a different ERC20 address.

For any calldata layout passed into the clone creation, the reference C.collateral() always returns the 20-byte address located at immutable arg offset 0x14, whereas the mutant returns the 20-byte address at 0x10 — therefore for all admissible immutable-arg byte arrays where the 20-byte words at offsets 0x10 and 0x14 are equal the reference and mutant agree, but there exist inputs where those two 20-byte words differ and the mutant returns a different address; the test constrains inputs so the reference's returned address equals the 20 bytes at offset 0x14 and detects when collateral() would differ if read at 0x10.

For any bytes20 a and bytes20 b placed into the clone's immutable args such that the 20 bytes at offset 0x14 equal a, the reference contract's collateral() always returns that address (a) for every input; the mutant that reads at 0x10 will return b when those 20 bytes at 0x10 differ, so there exist inputs where the mutant's collateral() != reference's collateral().

For any deployed reference C, collateral() always returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x14; the mutant that reads offset 0x10 can return a different address for some immutable-arg layouts, so there exist inputs where collateral() differs between reference and mutant.

For any deployed reference C clone, collateral() always returns the ERC20 address encoded at the immutable args offset 0x14; the mutant that reads offset 0x10 can return a different address for some immutable-arg layouts, so there exist inputs where the two implementations return different collateral addresses (the test fuzzes the two candidate addresses embedded into the clone creation payload and checks collateral() equals the expected offset-0x14 address).

For any deployed clean C instance, its collateral() getter returns the immutable argument placed at offset 0x14 (the second encoded address in the clone args); the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will return a different address for some valid immutable-arg payloads, so there exist inputs where collateral() differs between reference and mutant.

For any bytes-packed immutable args passed to the clone, the reference contract's collateral() always returns the second encoded address (offset 0x14), whereas the mutant reading offset 0x18 will differ for some packed inputs — so collateral() must equal the encoded address at offset 0x14 for all admissible inputs, a property the mutant can violate.

For any bytes immutable args passed into the clone creation, the correct contract's collateral() always returns the address encoded at offset 0x14 (the second encoded address); the mutant reading offset 0x18 will return a different address for some encoded payloads, so collateral() must equal the address at offset 0x14 for all admissible inputs and the mutant can violate this.

For any calldata-packed immutable args used by the clone, C.collateral() always returns the address encoded at offset 0x14 (the second encoded address); the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will return a different address for some inputs, so the property is broken by that mutant.

For any two addresses encoded as immutable args in the clone, the reference C.collateral() always returns the address placed at offset 0x14 (the second encoded address); the mutant that reads offset 0x18 will return a different address for some encodings, so collateral() == the second encoded address is a universal property the reference satisfies but the mutant can violate.

For every input, the reference contract's collateral() returns the immutable encoded collateral address (the 2nd immutable arg) whereas the mutant returns owner() instead—so the reference always returns an address != owner() whenever the encoded collateral arg != owner(), and the mutant breaks that by returning owner().

For any immutable constructor args, C.collateral() returns the encoded immutable collateral address (the second encoded arg) and thus equals address(c).collateral()'s underlying stored immutable value; the mutant returns owner() instead, so there exist inputs where collateral() != owner(), violating that rule.

For every deployment of C, collateral() returns an ERC20 address that is not equal to owner(); the mutant makes collateral() return owner(), so there exist deployments where collateral() == owner() causing the property to fail.

For any calldata-immutable encoding used by the reference C, collateral() returns the second immutable arg (an ERC20 address) which is never equal to owner() for at least some fuzzer-chosen immutable encoding; the mutant returns owner() instead, so there exist inputs where collateral() == owner() and thus the reference's property that collateral() != owner() for that input is violated by the mutant.

For any deployed C, collateral() returns an ERC20 address different from owner(); the mutant makes collateral() return owner(), so there exist inputs where collateral() == owner() and thus the property is broken.

For every deployed C the collateral() getter must return the immutable ERC20 address encoded at deployment (i.e., not the zero address); the mutant returns address(0) breaking this when the stored immutable is non-zero.
For any deployed C, collateral() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (the stored immutable); the mutant that always returns address(0) violates this for some deployments where the immutable is non-zero.

For any deployed C instance its collateral() getter returns the ERC20 address encoded in its immutable args (thus is non-zero whenever that immutable differs from zero); the mutant always returns address(0) breaking this when the immutable stored collateral is non-zero.

For any deployed C, calling collateral() returns an ERC20 whose address equals the stored immutable argument provided at deployment (i.e., collateral() != address(0) whenever the immutable arg is non-zero); the mutant always returns address(0) and thus violates this when the stored immutable collateral is non-zero, so there exists inputs (non-zero immutable arg) distinguishing them.

For any deployed C instance, collateral() returns a nonzero ERC20 address exactly when the immutable collateral arg passed at deployment is nonzero (the reference exposes the stored immutable, the mutant always returns address(0) and thus will produce a zero return for some deployments where the stored immutable is nonzero).

For any calldata/environment the reference contract's debt() getter returns the ERC20 address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x28 (the third address in the immutable args blob), whereas the mutant returns the address read 4 bytes later (0x2c) — so the reference always returns the exact address placed at offset 0x28 while the mutant can return a different address for some inputs.

For any calldata blob of immutable args (any bytes), C.debt() returns the address encoded at offset 0x28 (third 32-byte slot) — the mutant reads from 0x2c (shifted by 4 bytes) so for some immutables the returned address differs; the test encodes arbitrary immutable args and asserts the reference's returned address equals the address encoded at offset 0x28.

For any immutable-args byte blob, the reference C.debt() returns the address encoded at immutable arg offset 0x28 (the third address slot); the mutant shifts the read by 4 bytes (0x2c) and thus will return a different address for some immutable blobs, so the property is that debt() == address decoded from calldata-immediate-slot-0x28.

For any calldata/immutable-args blob, C.debt() returns the address encoded at immutable-arg offset 0x28 (the third address slot); the mutant reads from 0x2c (shifted 4 bytes) so for some immutable blobs the returned address differs and the property is violated.

For any immutable-args blob used to deploy the clone, the correct C.debt() always returns the address encoded at immutable offset 0x28 (the third 32-byte slot); the mutant misreads at 0x2c and therefore for some immutable blobs will return a different address.

For any input, the reference contract's debt() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (the immutable argument), whereas the mutant returns address(0) for some inputs; thus calling debt() should always return a non-zero address in the correct contract but can be zero in the buggy one.

For every deployment the correct contract's debt() returns a non-zero ERC20 address (reads an immutable arg), whereas the mutant can return the zero address; the test asserts debt() != address(0) for all fuzzed inputs.
